details:
**"You who hear the sound, in scattered rhymes" / Il Canzoniere**
This line opens Petrarch's collection of 366 Italian vernacular poems, mostly sonnets. Its Latin title is *Rerum vulgarium fragmenta*, and it is also known as *Rime sparse* ("scattered rhymes") or *Il Canzoniere* ("The Songbook"). It became the model for European love poetry for centuries.

**Laura, met on Good Friday in Avignon**
Laura is the woman to whom Petrarch addressed most of the Canzoniere. He first saw her on Good Friday, April 6, 1327, at the church of Sainte-Claire in Avignon. She was already married and never returned his love. She is often identified as Laura de Noves, wife of Count Hugues de Sade.

**Petrarchan sonnet (octave + sestet)**
This fourteen-line form is named for Petrarch. It divides into an eight-line octave, usually rhymed ABBAABBA, which poses a problem or emotion. A six-line sestet follows, turning or resolving it, after a shift called the *volta*. It is also called the Italian sonnet, in contrast to the Shakespearean sonnet with its final couplet.

**Africa (epic on Scipio Africanus)**
Petrarch's unfinished Latin epic in hexameters covers the Second Punic War. It centers on Scipio Africanus's defeat of Hannibal at the Battle of Zama. It opens with "Scipio's Dream" and includes episodes such as Syphax's palace, the death of Sophonisba, and the dying lament of Hannibal's brother Mago. Petrarch was crowned poet laureate partly on the strength of this work.

**"The Ascent of Mont Ventoux"**
This letter, collected in the *Epistolae Familiares*, describes Petrarch's climb of a mountain in Provence with his brother Gherardo, ignoring an old shepherd's warnings. At the summit he opens Augustine's *Confessions* at random and rebukes himself for "admiring earthly things," since "nothing is wonderful but the soul." He claims to be the first person since antiquity to climb a mountain just for the view. The letter is addressed to Dionigi da Borgo San Sepolcro, later Bishop of Monopoli.

**Triumphs (Trionfi)**
This allegorical vernacular poem presents a dream vision of six successive triumphal processions, in which each figure conquers the one before. The order is Love, Chastity, Death, Fame, Time, and Eternity. The vision begins in Valchiusa (Vaucluse), where the sleeping poet sees Love pass in a chariot. Chastity, led by Laura with virtuous women such as Lucretia and Penelope, binds Love to a column. In the Triumph of Death, Death plucks a golden hair from Laura's head.

**Secretum (My Secret Book)**
This Latin dialogue between Petrarch and Saint Augustine is witnessed by the silent personification Lady Truth. Augustine criticizes Petrarch's love for Laura and his pursuit of fame. He says that accidie (spiritual listlessness) binds Petrarch's will in "adamantine chains." The work was not meant for publication during Petrarch's lifetime.

**On Illustrious Men (De viris illustribus)**
This is Petrarch's unfinished Latin collection of biographies, modeled on Plutarch's *Parallel Lives*. It profiles mainly Roman heroes, along with biblical and mythical figures such as Romulus and Hercules. Many of the same figures appear in *Africa*.

**"The world's delight is a brief dream"**
This line closes the opening sonnet of the Canzoniere. In that poem Petrarch recalls "those sighs on which I fed my heart" during his "first youthful error." He admits he has become "an old tale" among the people, so that "shame is the fruit of my vanities." He also hopes to find "pity, and forgiveness" for all the ways he talks and weeps.

**"The sun's ray was darkened in pity for its Maker"**
This line comes from Canzoniere Sonnet 3, which recounts falling in love with Laura on Good Friday. The sun dimmed in mourning for Christ's crucifixion. On that day Love found the poet "weaponless" and captured him through Laura's "lovely eyes."

**Letter to Posterity**
This autobiographical letter by Petrarch concludes his late letter collection, the *Seniles*. Petrarch's letter collections (*Familiares* and *Seniles*) were inspired by his 1345 discovery of Cicero's letters to Atticus in Verona. He dedicated the *Familiares* to his friend "Socrates" (Ludwig van Kempen).

**Thomas Wyatt and the Earl of Surrey translations**
These Tudor poets brought the Petrarchan sonnet to England. Wyatt's "Whoso List to Hunt" adapts Petrarch's sonnet of a white deer whose collar reads "Noli me tangere" ("touch me not"). Surrey translated a line as "Love that doth reign and live within my thought."

**"In Life" and "In Death" / Prayer to the Virgin**
The Canzoniere is divided into two parts: poems written during Laura's life and poems after her death in the plague of 1348. The collection ends with a canzone, "Prayer to the Virgin." In it Petrarch asks to "die in peaceful harbor" and to let his "vanishing, at least, be virtuous."

**"Golden hair scattered in the breeze"**
This image comes from the sonnet "Erano i capei d'oro a l'aura sparsi." In it Laura's gold hair is twined by the wind "in a thousand sweet knots." The phrase "l'aura" ("the breeze") is a pun on Laura's name, a wordplay Petrarch uses throughout the collection.

**Coronation Oration**
Petrarch delivered this speech on Rome's Capitoline Hill in 1341, when he was crowned poet laureate. It was the first such coronation since antiquity. Petrarch is also credited with coining the concept of the "Dark Ages" for the period after Rome's fall.
